Drafting:
Tides are the rhythmic rising and falling of ocean waters, a phenomenon driven primarily by the gravitational interaction between the Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. The Moon, being the closest celestial body, exerts the strongest influence on our planet's tides. Its gravity pulls on the Earth, and because gravity weakens with distance, the water on the side of the Earth facing the Moon is pulled more strongly than the solid earth itself, creating a bulge. Simultaneously, on the opposite side of the Earth, a second bulge forms. This occurs because the Earth is pulled toward the Moon more strongly than the water on the far side, effectively leaving the water behind as the planet moves closer to the Moon. As the Earth rotates on its axis once every twenty-four hours, different parts of the planet move through these bulges, experiencing high tides, while areas between the bulges experience low tides.

The Sun also plays a significant role, though its effect is roughly half that of the Moon due to its immense distance. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth align, which happens during the new and full moon phases, their gravitational forces combine to create higher high tides and lower low tides, known as spring tides. Conversely, when they form a right angle relative to each other during the quarter moon phases, their gravitational pulls counteract each other slightly, resulting in neap tides with less extreme differences between high and low water levels. Local geography, such as the shape of coastlines and the depth of the ocean floor, further modifies these tidal patterns, causing tides to vary significantly from one location to another.
